http://mn.medstroms.se/hassela/firstpage.html
Hassela is based in the Stockholm City Hall and is obviously well funded. Their web site provides a wealth of information that is hard to find elsewhere. I have been negligent in not reporting on it before. They make no effort to hide their prohibitionist agenda. While they have an appalling lack of intellectual standards – as the review below demonstrates, they also seem unaware when the data they cite contradicts their own position – again as the review below demonstrates.

Marijuana Myths, Marijuana Facts by Zimmer and Morgan
See
JAMA Book Review: Marijuana Myths, Marijuana Facts -- "Extraordinarily Well-Researched And Passionately Argued" and
Marijuana Myths; Marijuana Facts Reviewed by Travis Charbeneau

- A Review by Janet D. Lapey, MD (Ed. note: Dr. Lapey has no particular credentials other than her medical degree, but she is often the "star-witness" for the prohibitionists at various hearings.)

Recently, a book entitled Marijuana Myths, Marijuana Facts has been receiving much publicity, especially by drug-legalizers such as William F. Buckley, Jr. It should be noted that the book's authors, Lynn Zimmer and John Morgan, serve on the Board of Directors of the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws (NORML), a group which advocates the legalization of marijuana. Furthermore, their 1997 book is published by The Lindesmith Center, a New York pro-drug legalization organization funded by George Soros. (Ed. note: Hassela seems obsessed with Soros. They carry regular stories about his rumored financial deals. An odd focus for a site supposedly devoted to "Drug" issues.)

The authors' blatant pro-marijuana bias is described in a review in Science, October 3, 1997, by Wayne Hall of the Australian National Drug and Alcohol Research Center. (Ed. note: One wonders if Dr. Lapey actually read the book herself. This review seems to be based on a review.

Zimmer and Morgan attempt to minimize marijuana's addictive potential. Hall states that readers must not be distracted from "the fact that a minority of users (perhaps 10 percent of those who ever use and more of those who use regularly) do experience difficulties in controlling their use. They use more marijuana than they would like to, continue to use it to the detriment of their physical health and well-being, find it difficult to stop, and are seeking help in increasing numbers. It would be remarkable if marijuana did not have a dependency potential given that it is widely used like alcohol for its euphoric and relaxing effects. Honesty demands that the risk of dependence be acknowledged, even if it may be used by the authors' opponents to argue for continuation of prohibition."

In addition, Hall states that it is wrong to say that marijuana smoking is benign, given the fact that marijuana smokers may smoke daily for decades and given the fact that "there are strong similarities between the carcinogenic and toxic constituents of tobacco and marijuana smoke." Hall also observes that the adverse public health impact of marijuana would surely increase "if its use increased under a legal regime which allowed its widespread promotion, sale, and use." Hall concludes that readers who want a disinterested appraisal of the most probable health hazards of long-term daily marijuana use will not find this book useful.

Zimmer and Morgan also downplay studies of the harmful effects of marijuana on the immune system. For instance, Baldwin et al reported that the pulmonary white blood cells (alveolar macrophages) of people who smoke marijuana have decreased ability to engulf and kill both bacteria and tumor cells and produce lower amounts of substances necessary for the immune response (Am J Respir Crit Care Med 156:1606-1613, 1997). This may explain the fact that HIV-positive marijuana smokers have an increased risk of bacterial pneumonia, as reported by Caiaffa et al in the same scientific journal in 1994.

Furthermore, Marijuana Myths, Marijuana Facts contains inaccurate material. The authors try to blame the increased risk of bacterial pneumonia in marijuana smokers on other drugs, such as crack. They incorrectly claim (p. 110) that the majority of the marijuana smokers had actually smoked three illicit drugs: marijuana, cocaine, and crack. However, Caiaffa et al clearly state that out of 77 who reported their smoking habits, 87.9% used marijuana, 25.9% cocaine, and 9.1% crack. (Ed. note: What they actually said was "most had smoked all three illicit drugs and the vast majority also smoked tobacco." This is one of hundreds of citations.)

Caiaffa et al found that the odds of developing bacterial pneumonia were nearly twice as high in illicit drug smokers, including the majority who smoked marijuana but not crack or cocaine. In other words, marijuana smoking is especially dangerous in HIV-infected persons since it increases the likelihood that they will develop pneumonia.

As Hall indicates, Morgan and Zimmer's book is not for those who are looking for a non-biased report of marijuana's effects. Just as it would be unwise to rely on the tobacco lobby to provide accurate information about the harmful effects of tobacco, it is pure folly to rely on the drug legalization lobby to provide accurate information about marijuana. (Dr. Morgan told me that for several years he had been intending to join NORML, but was finally spurred to do so when he kept being falsely "accused" of being a member by prohibitionists. He later joined the board of directors. Perhaps NORML owes Dr. Lapey and other prohibitionists thanks for having Dr. Morgan as a member.)
